examGuide.title: Approach the exam question
examGuide.body: Identify all candidate keys and prime attributes first. BCNF requires every nontrivial determinant to be a superkey. 3NF also permits a prime attribute on the right. 2NF forbids a nonprime attribute depending on a proper subset of any candidate key. Atomic values establish 1NF, not higher forms.

examGuide.title: Worked problem
examGuide.body:
R(A,B,C) has A→B and B→C, with A its only candidate key. How many listed dependencies violate BCNF?

**Answer: 1.** A→B has a superkey determinant and is allowed. B→C has a determinant B whose closure is {B,C}, missing A, so it violates BCNF. Exactly one listed dependency violates it; it also violates 3NF because C is nonprime.

examGuide.title: Conditions and edge cases
examGuide.body:
A relation can have several candidate keys. Checking only the designated primary key can miss partial dependencies or prime-attribute exceptions.

3NF permits a non-superkey determinant when the dependent attribute is prime; BCNF does not.
